questions.q: Two small charged bodies are brought near one another. Which statement correctly summarises the directions of the electric forces between charges?
options: Like charges attract one another and unlike charges repel one another
Like charges repel one another and unlike charges attract one another
All charges, whether like or unlike, attract one another
Only charges of different magnitude exert forces on each other
questions.explanation: Two positive charges repel one another, two negative charges repel one another, but a positive charge and a negative charge attract one another. This is summarised as: like charges repel; unlike charges attract — the fundamental rule everything in electrostatics rests on.

questions.q: A neutral body becomes negatively charged. Identify what has happened to the body in terms of its electrons and protons.
options: It has gained protons, giving it an excess of protons
It has lost protons, leaving a deficiency of protons
It has gained electrons, giving it an excess of electrons
It has lost electrons, leaving a deficiency of electrons
questions.explanation: A body that gains electrons has more electrons than protons — an excess of electrons — and is negatively charged. It is always electrons that are gained or lost, because the protons are strongly bound in the nuclei at the centres of the atoms.

questions.q: A body has a positive charge of +4.60 μC. Calculate how many electrons the body is deficient by, given the charge on one electron is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
working: Since the body is positively charged, it has a deficiency of electrons.
questions.explanation: Because charge is quantised in whole multiples of the elementary charge, the number of electrons is simply the total charge divided by the charge on one electron. A positive body has a deficiency (shortage) of electrons.

questions.q: State Coulomb's Law for the electrostatic force between two point charges at rest.
options: The force is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
The force is inversely proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the distance between them
The force is directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance between them
The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance between them
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law: the force between two charges at rest is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, giving \(F = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r^2}\) with \(k \approx 9.0\times10^9\,\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}\). Distance is squared, so it is an inverse-square law just like gravity.

questions.q: Two point charges, each of +2.0 × 10⁻⁵ C, are placed 0.30 m apart. Using Coulomb's Law with k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², calculate the magnitude of the electrostatic force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive.
working: Both charges have the same (positive) sign, so the force is repulsive.
questions.explanation: Substitute the two charges and the separation, square the distance, then check the signs. Same-sign charges give a repulsive force pushing them apart.

questions.q: How is the magnitude of the electric field strength E at a point defined?
options: The total force exerted by all the charges in the region
The force per unit charge experienced by a charge placed at the point, E = F/q
The product of the force and the charge at the point, E = Fq
The charge per unit force at the point, E = q/F
questions.explanation: The magnitude of the electric field strength is found by putting a charge q at the point and measuring the force F the field exerts on it, giving E = F/q, with SI unit newton per coulomb (N C⁻¹). The field is a property of the location and exists whether or not a charge is placed there.

questions.q: Describe the pattern of electric field lines surrounding a single negative point charge.
options: The lines point radially outward, away from the charge, and may cross one another
The lines point radially inward, towards the charge, and never cross one another
The lines form closed loops around the charge with no beginning or end
The lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced in one direction
questions.explanation: A positive test charge placed near a negative point charge feels a force towards it, so the field — and the field lines — point radially inward towards −Q. Lines start on positive charges and end on negative charges, and they never cross because the field can have only one direction at each point.

questions.q: Two parallel plates are separated by 0.020 m with a potential difference of 100 V between them. Calculate the strength of the uniform electric field between the plates.
working: For a uniform field between parallel plates, \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\)
questions.explanation: Between parallel plates the field is uniform, so dividing the voltage by the plate separation gives the field strength. This gives a second, equivalent unit for electric field — volts per metre, the same as newtons per coulomb.

questions.q: From memory, explain what is meant by the conservation of electric charge, including what happens to the total charge when two charged conductors are brought into contact.
keyPoints: The total amount of electric charge never changes — electric charge is conserved; it can only be transferred from one body to another.
When two previously neutral bodies are charged by friction, the positive charge on one equals the negative charge on the other.
When two charged conductors are brought into contact there is a redistribution of charge, but the total amount of charge remains the same.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that charge is only transferred (never created or destroyed) and that the total stays constant on contact, grade yourself Good or Easy. This is the same kind of conservation law as conservation of energy and momentum.

questions.q: From memory, distinguish between charging a neutral conductor by conduction and by induction, including the final sign of the charge in each case relative to the charging object.
keyPoints: Conduction (contact): the charged object touches the conductor; charge is shared on contact, so the conductor ends up with the SAME sign as the charging object.
Induction (no contact): the charged object is brought near but does not touch; its field separates the charges, the conductor is earthed, then the earth and charging object are removed.
Induction leaves the conductor with the OPPOSITE sign to the charging object — without ever touching it.
questions.explanation: The classic discriminator: conduction = contact = same sign; induction = no contact = opposite sign. Mixing these up is the single most common electrostatics error.
